name: inline-message
intent: Give a single message send its own intention-revealing one-line method - the message pattern written without explicit line breaks - so callers read intent instead of the delegated expression and have one name to reuse, override and test.
problem: An operation that is really one delegation is expressed at every call site as a raw expression or a chain of sends: it has no name to reuse, override, mock or document, the same expression is duplicated, and a change to the delegated call means finding every copy. Adding a named method is the fix, yet a one-line method is easy to dismiss as a useless pass-through, and its selector is often wrapped over several lines - so the 'improvement' costs more vertical space than the single line of body it contains.
context: Method-scale work in object-oriented and procedural codebases: a class composes a collaborator it forwards to (wrapper, facade, adapter, decorator, application service over a repository), callers repeat the same low-level expression, and the house style favours small Composed Methods. The formatting half of the pattern presumes a message-pattern syntax (keyword selectors or long parameter lists) plus an editor or IDE that shows the selector next to the body, so a long selector can be reformatted without hiding the operation name.
benefits: Call sites read as intent: the selector carries the meaning, and the reader no longer decodes the forwarded expression or re-derives what it accomplishes.
One expression, one name, one place to change: the operation can be reused, overridden, documented and tested in isolation, and a fix to the delegated call is a one-line edit.
Vertical space is spent on behaviour: writing the message pattern without explicit line breaks keeps Composed Methods within a screenful, so navigation and review stay cheap.
A uniform delegation surface: wrapper and facade classes that forward several members stay scannable when every member is exactly one message send.
The smallest useful seam: the one-liner is the cheapest place to add logging, caching, lazy initialization or a guard later, without touching a single call site.
tradeoffs: Indirection: every one-liner adds a name to maintain, a frame in stack traces and one navigation hop for readers; a class whose methods are all forwarders is the Middle Man smell.
The naming decision is the hard part: a selector that merely restates the delegate's own name buys no information and must be renamed later with tool support across every call site.

One line can be too short: with many keyword arguments the message pattern exceeds a comfortable width, and breaking it into one keyword per line hands back exactly the vertical space the pattern exists to save.
Debugging and profiling noise: forwarding frames appear in stack traces and profiles, and teams working on latency must exclude or collapse them before a profile becomes readable.

A forwarder also hides: once callers go through the wrapper they cannot reach the delegate directly, so widening the surface later means adding members one at a time, and drift between wrapper and delegate is invisible until it is used.

participants.responsibility: Calls the named message instead of the raw expression; reads only the intent the selector states and does not need to know which collaborator performs the work.
The one-line method itself: an intention-revealing selector whose whole body is a single message send to the delegate, written without explicit line breaks.
The composed collaborator that performs the operation; it stays unaware of the forwarding method and can be substituted as long as the message signature holds.

use_cases: Wrapper, adapter, decorator and facade classes: each published member forwards to the wrapped object in one line, so the wrapper's surface is the only thing a reader must scan.
Value and domain types: Money#plus or Duration#shift is one send to the underlying representation, keeping call sites inside the domain's own vocabulary.
Service layering: an application service names a use case (cancelOrder) and forwards to the repository or domain object that implements it.
Test doubles and seams: an interaction that is one named message is trivially stubbed, while the same interaction written as an expression cannot be intercepted.
Formatting for review: keeping every selector on one line so a small method still fits a diff hunk and the code-review pane without scrolling.
API client wrappers: a typed HTTP client that composes a lower-level fetch function and names each endpoint method so the wrapper's surface is the only thing callers see.
Framework adapters: a persistence repository that forwards to an ORM session while naming each query after the domain question it answers.
Microservice facades: a BFF (Backend for Frontend) that composes several downstream services and exposes one named method per use-case rather than exposing every downstream call.

Python's logging.LoggerAdapter wraps a Logger and forwards the familiar logging methods while adding contextual fields, making a context-aware logger a named seam rather than repeated low-level logging setup.

A Go client wrapper can expose one-line domain operations over net/http.Client while keeping the injected RoundTripper/Transport behind the wrapper; the standard library documents that Client delegates request execution to that transport.

ASP.NET Core IHttpClientFactory composes named DelegatingHandler instances over an inner handler, so each policy or endpoint adapter can expose only the intention-bearing one-send methods callers need.
avoid_when: The name would just repeat the delegate's own selector (wrapper.add calling list.add): call the delegate directly - that one-liner is a Middle Man, not a message with meaning.
The body is not a single message send: a condition, a loop, a second statement or a temporary variable belongs to Composed Method, not to this pattern.
The selector genuinely needs several lines (many long keyword arguments in a narrow window): reduce the arity with a Parameter Object or accept the break rather than fighting the formatter.
The forwarded name would leak a collaborator the caller must not know about (Law of Demeter): change the caller's question instead of inserting another proxy hop.
The operation is a hot path in a runtime that cannot inline or devirtualize the extra hop: measure first, and collapse the wrapper only where the profile says so.
anti_patterns: Forwarding spam: a whole class of one-liners that only rename the delegate's members (Middle Man), growing the surface without adding information.
Keyword-per-line selectors: 'formatting for readability' by breaking the message pattern across lines, spending the vertical space the pattern exists to save.
Misleading names: a one-liner whose selector suggests a query but forwards a mutation, so the caller's code reads well and behaves wrongly.
Hop chains: a.cancel() forwarding to b.cancel() forwarding to c.cancel(), three files and three names for one operation, each adding a frame and a place to change.

Remote proxy as local forwarder: forwarding an HTTP or gRPC call inside a one-liner hides latency, retryability and failure modes from callers who read the wrapper's intent-bearing name as a cheap local call.
design_principles: Intention-revealing names: the selector, not the expression, states what the operation means (the companion Intention Revealing Message / Selector patterns).
Single responsibility at member granularity: a body that is exactly one message send cannot hide a second task.
DRY and a single point of change: one expression, one name, one place to edit, override or mock.
Separation of interface and implementation: callers depend on the named message rather than on the delegate's surface.
Least indirection: pay for a new name only when the name adds information; otherwise delete the method.
best_practices: Name the method after the intent, not the mechanism; if the best available name is the delegate's own selector, do not add the method.
Write the message pattern without explicit line breaks; if it will not fit, reduce the arity (Parameter Object) or split the operation instead of breaking the line.
Keep the body exactly one message send - no conditionals, temporaries or second statement; grow it into a Composed Method when it needs more.
Inject the delegate (constructor parameter or field) instead of looking it up or creating it in the body, so the one-liner remains substitutable and testable.
Delete forwarders that no longer earn their name: they surface as Middle Man in review and should not be kept just in case.
Let the name state the effect: a forwarding selector is a contract, and the forwarded call must honour it (a query name over a mutation is a lie).

Choose hand-written one-liners when each forwarded operation needs its own name for reuse, override, mocking or documentation; prefer bulk delegation (language features or meta-programming) only when the set of forwarded members is large or frequently changing and the wrapper adds no per-member behaviour.
Avoid the shadowing trap: a forwarding method whose name matches the delegate's own selector is a Middle Man; use the delegate directly or rename to express the intent the wrapper adds.

Keep delegation explicit in types: make the delegate a named field or constructor parameter so its interface is a visible part of the wrapper's public API, not an implementation detail that callers accidentally depend on.
sources: Beck, K., Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns, Volume 1: Coding, Prentice Hall, 1997 - Inline Message Pattern (Formatting chapter, pp. 172-174; draft p. 127): 'Write the message pattern without explicit line breaks.' Companion patterns cited there: Delegation, Simple Delegation, Intention Revealing Selector.

Fowler, M., Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley, 2018 — Inline Method (opposite of Extract Method): 'When a method body is more obvious than the method itself, replace usages with the method body.' https://refactoring.guru/inline-method

JetBrains ReSharper, 'Inline Method' refactoring — replaces method usages with the method body; available for C#, VB.NET, and other languages via the IntelliJ platform. https://www.jetbrains.com/help/resharper/Refactorings__Inline_Method.html
Microsoft Learn, 'Inline Method' refactoring (Visual Studio 2022+) — Quick Actions and Refactorings menu for C# and VB. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/ide/reference/inline-method

Weir, C., 'Beck 1997 — Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns', Pattern Almanac 2019 — confirms pp. 172-174 with the formatting rule 'To format the message pattern, avoid explicit line breaks.' https://smallmemory.charlesweir.com/almanac/almanac/Beck97.html

The Go Programming Language: 'Forwarding methods' section — struct embedding promotes methods of the embedded type, explicitly naming this delegation/forwarding. https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#interfaces_and_methods

Rust std::ops::Deref — 'Implement Deref or DerefMut if a value transparently behaves like a value of the target type'; documents the trait's role in delegation patterns. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Deref.html

Python documentation, 'object.__getattr__' — called only when the attribute is not found through the normal lookup chain, enabling transparent delegation proxies. https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__getattr__
